plan: New informational essay (CLD-P-ACT-E-000004) weighted toward Production of Writing and Knowledge of Language (under-represented), with NO CHANGE keyed twice and balanced choice lengths.

passages.title: The Seed Library

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: patrons could check up a packet of seeds
candidates.explanation: Borrowing an item from a library is to "check out" the item.

A.rationale: "Check up" means to investigate, not to borrow.

D.rationale: "Check off" means to mark an item on a list.

hints: What do library patrons do with books they borrow?

strategy.explanation: Supply the idiom yourself, then match.

candidates.remember: Phrasal verbs change meaning with the small word.

candidates.subskill: Deciding whether to keep a sentence
candidates.stem: The writer is considering deleting the underlined sentence. Should the sentence be kept or deleted?

choices.A: Kept, because it gives a detail about the collection's origins that the essay returns to later.
choices.B: Kept, because it explains why the librarians doubted that anyone would use the seed library.
choices.C: Deleted, because it shifts the focus of the paragraph from the library to farming in general.
choices.D: Deleted, because it repeats information already given in the paragraph's previous sentence.

candidates.evidence: the farmer's beans, which reliably breed true, became the most popular
candidates.explanation: The sentence introduces the retired farmer who donated most of the seeds; paragraph 3 refers back to "the farmer's beans," which would make no sense without it.

B.rationale: The sentence is about the catalog's source and gives no reason for the librarians' doubt.

C.rationale: The sentence stays focused on the library's collection.

D.rationale: The previous sentence explains how borrowing works; it says nothing about the catalog or donor.

hints: Does any later sentence depend on this one?
Look for "the farmer" later in the essay.

strategy.explanation: Search the rest of the essay for a reference that depends on this sentence.

candidates.remember: Keep a sentence that later text depends on.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: only a dozen patrons borrowed seeds
candidates.explanation: A dozen borrowers the first year contrasts with more than three hundred packets the next, so a contrast transition is needed: "However."

A.rationale: Rapid growth is not a result of a slow first spring.

C.rationale: The two years are different, not similar.

D.rationale: The second sentence is not an example of the first.

hints: Compare a dozen borrowers with three hundred packets.

strategy.explanation: Decide the relationship (contrast) before reading choices.

candidates.remember: Name the relationship first, then pick the transition.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.explanation: The teachers belong to two schools, so the plural possessive "schools'" is needed; "teachers" is simply plural and needs no apostrophe.

A.rationale: "Schools" needs an apostrophe to show possession.

B.rationale: "School's" is singular, but "Both" refers to two schools.

C.rationale: "Teachers'" adds a possessive that nothing follows.

hints: Do the teachers own anything in this sentence?

strategy.explanation: Check each noun: is it plural, possessive, or both?

candidates.remember: Plural possessive: add the apostrophe after the s.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: Students who planted the seeds at home
candidates.explanation: The subject "Students" (modified by "who planted the seeds at home") needs a main verb; "brought" supplies it.

A.rationale: "Bringing" is not a main verb, so the sentence is a fragment.

B.rationale: "And bringing" still leaves the subject without a main verb.

D.rationale: "Having brought" is a participle, not a main verb.

hints: Is "planted" the main verb, or part of a who-clause?

strategy.explanation: Strike the who-clause and see what verb the subject needs.

candidates.remember: A who-clause verb is not the sentence's main verb.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: some vegetables, such as squash, cross-pollinate easily
candidates.explanation: "Such as squash" is a nonessential example set off by a pair of commas; the comma before "such" requires the closing comma after "squash."

B.rationale: Without the closing comma, the opening comma before "such" is left unpaired.

C.rationale: A comma should not separate "such as" from its example.

D.rationale: A semicolon would split the subject from its verb.

hints: Is there a comma before "such as"?
Could the sentence work without "such as squash"?

strategy.explanation: Nonessential phrases need commas on both sides.

candidates.remember: Interrupting phrases take a pair of commas.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.B: These seeds can produce offspring that look unlike their parent plants.
choices.C: Gardeners learned, in other words, that such seeds could be unpredictable.

candidates.evidence: so seeds saved from them may not grow true to the parent plant
candidates.explanation: The previous sentence already says the seeds may not grow true to the parent plant; every version of this sentence repeats that point.

A.rationale: It restates the previous sentence's point.

B.rationale: Shorter, but still repeats the previous sentence.

C.rationale: "In other words" admits that it only restates the point.

hints: What does the previous sentence already say?

strategy.explanation: If every version only repeats, delete it.

candidates.remember: Delete sentences that only restate the one before.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: Today the seed library circulates more than a thousand packets a year
candidates.explanation: The shelves belong to the seed library (singular), so the possessive "Its" is correct.

C.rationale: "Their" is plural, but the seed library is singular.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.B: corn, a variety of it that the town's founders grew and that had nearly been lost
choices.C: a nearly lost corn variety that the town's founders grew

candidates.evidence: a variety of corn which was grown by the founders of the town and which had nearly been lost entirely
candidates.explanation: C keeps all the information (grown by the founders, nearly lost) in the fewest words.

A.rationale: Wordy: two "which" clauses and "entirely" add length without meaning.

B.rationale: Still wordy, and "of it" is awkward.

D.rationale: Too short: it drops the information that the variety is historic and was nearly lost.

hints: Which choice keeps every fact in the fewest words?

strategy.explanation: Shortest choice that keeps the meaning.

candidates.remember: Concise is best only if no meaning is lost.

candidates.subskill: Conclusion that returns to the opening
candidates.stem: Which choice most effectively concludes the essay by returning to an idea from its opening?

choices.B: Several other libraries in the state have since started seed libraries.
choices.C: Heirloom vegetables are often prized by gardeners for their flavor.
choices.D: The library also lends cake pans, telescopes, and fishing rods.

candidates.evidence: the librarians were not sure anyone would use it
candidates.explanation: The essay opens with the librarians unsure anyone would use the seed library; the current sentence answers that doubt.

B.rationale: It extends the story outward but does not return to the opening.

C.rationale: It comments on heirlooms, not on the opening idea.

hints: What doubt does the first sentence express?

strategy.explanation: The stem names the goal: tie back to the opening.

candidates.remember: When asked to echo the opening, reread the first sentence.

candidates.stem:
The writer is considering adding the following sentence after the second sentence of the last paragraph:
"Corn is one of the most widely grown crops in the world."
Should the writer make this addition there?

choices.A: Yes, because it explains why that variety of corn had nearly been lost.
choices.B: No, because it adds a general fact that distracts from the library's collection.
choices.C: Yes, because it emphasizes how valuable the library's collection has become.
choices.D: No, because it contradicts the claim that the corn variety was nearly lost.

candidates.evidence: Today the seed library circulates more than a thousand packets a year
candidates.explanation: The paragraph describes the seed library's current collection; a world fact about corn is off topic.

A.rationale: Corn being widely grown does not explain why one variety was nearly lost.

C.rationale: A fact about corn worldwide says nothing about this collection's value.

D.rationale: A crop can be widespread while one variety of it is rare, so there is no contradiction.

hints: Does a world statistic about corn serve that?

strategy.explanation: Check whether the sentence serves the paragraph's focus.

candidates.remember: Added sentences must serve the paragraph's focus.

candidates.subskill: Evaluating whether an essay meets a goal
candidates.stem: Suppose the writer's goal had been to write an essay explaining how to save seeds from garden vegetables. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.A: Yes, because it explains which vegetables breed true and which do not.
choices.B: Yes, because it describes how patrons return saved seeds each fall.
choices.C: No, because it argues that most seed libraries fail in their first year.
choices.D: No, because it mainly recounts how one library's seed program grew.

candidates.evidence: The first spring, only a dozen patrons borrowed seeds.
candidates.explanation: The essay tells the history of one library's seed program; it never explains the steps for saving seeds.

A.rationale: It mentions that some plants cross-pollinate but gives no seed-saving method.

B.rationale: It says seeds are returned, not how to save them.

C.rationale: The essay describes this program's success, not a failure.

hints: What is the essay mostly about?

strategy.explanation: State the essay's purpose, then compare with the goal.

candidates.remember: Judge a goal against the essay's main focus.
